newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Defence ministers meet to discuss NATO reforms. [CORRECTED 16:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Defence ministers meet to discuss NATO reforms. [CORRECTED 16:43 GMT]

text.p: NATO defence ministers meet on Thursday (corrects day from Wednesday) to review plans to overhaul the alliance's command structures, but plans to give the Europeans a greater say have been thrown into doubt by the French Socialists' election win.
"Whatever happens now must be a provisional solution," said one alliance official.

NATO, which this summer is set to invite some former communist countries to join the alliance, has been working on reforms to bring the West's defence grouping into line with the realities of the post-Cold War world.

The plan is to make the alliance more flexible and able to carry out new types of mission, such as the current peace operation in Bosnia, and save money by cutting a number of commands, no longer considered vital.

France, which left the alliance's military wing in 1966, has also pushed for the creation of a separate European identity within NATO, effectively dropping plans to try to create a defence role within the European Union.

Two years ago French President Jacques Chirac, drawing on the lessons of Bosnia and the Gulf War, where France initially had problems working alongside its allies, said Paris would reintegrate into an alliance with a greater European identity.

But Chirac, who faced strong domestic opposition over the issue, said he wanted certain key commands -- most notably the strategic southern command at Naples -- to come under a European rather than U.S. commander.

Alliance sources say Chirac had not received sufficient concessions from Washington to proceed and announce his country's reintegration into a "new NATO" to be launched at a summit in Madrid on July 8-9.

But France's election, which brought to power a Socialist government under Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, suspicious of perceived U.S. dominance in the alliance, has further reduced his room for manoeuvre.

"I think Chirac had decided to put everything on hold anyway, but now there is virtually no question about it. What now remains is to see how much we can do without France," said one military official.

The Madrid summit is set to invite at least Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance, create a new forum for partnership countries and adopt the more flexible and streamlined command structure.

NATO officials say it is possible to imagine a European identity without France, but add that in reality it would be a pale imitation of what was originally conceived -- particularly the idea of European-only operations using NATO equipment.
"Clearly a reformed command structure for a new NATO without the participation of the second largest and most important army in the alliance would not be satisfactory," added the official.

Military analysts say plans to use the Western European Union (WEU), the EU's designated defence grouping, to run limited Europe-only missions with NATO's help were drawn up on the assumption France would be involved.

The ministers will also review the current situation in Bosnia ahead of key municipal elections later this year and the failure to make any progress in persuading the respective parties to hand over indicted war criminals.
